extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers, students and scholars of political philosophy and law, and policymakers interested in free speech and individual liberty
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on when opinions and actions should be free, the limits of that freedom (harm/incitement), and the moral norms of public discussion and individual self-development. Targets principles for free expression, limits on legal restraint, and the value of individuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possibility of truth in silenced opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: If any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not silence opinions on the assumption they are false; legal or social suppression risks excluding true views. This is a fundamental justification for permissive protection of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of collision of adverse opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions, that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing competing opinions to contend enables discovery and correction of incomplete prevailing opinions. Suppressing minority errors may also suppress useful partial truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of contestation to prevent dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will, by most of those who receive it, be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular, vigorous debate keeps doctrines understood and alive; without contest they calcify into prejudice or hollow ritual. This is a reason to permit contest even of widely accepted truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of legal restraint: misrepresentation and incitement, not mere intemperance
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal offences ... are to argue sophistically, to suppress facts or arguments, to misstate the elements of the case, or misrepresent the opposite opinion. But all this ... is so continually done in perfect good faith ... that it is rarely possible on adequate grounds conscientiously to stamp the misrepresentation as morally culpable; and still less could law presume to interfere with this kind of controversial misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law should not police mere intemperate language (invective, sarcasm, personality); it should only intervene where discussion involves deliberate misrepresentation, sophistry, suppression of facts, or where expression constitutes a direct and provable harm. Social/opinion sanction, rather than legal coercion, is the appropriate check for much controversial misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of immunity when expression incites imminent harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions lose their immunity when the circumstances in which they are expressed are such as to constitute their expression a positive instigation to some mischievous act. An opinion that corn-dealers are starvers of the poor ... may justly incur punishment when delivered orally to an excited mob assembled before the house of a corn-dealer, or when handed about among the same mob in the form of a placard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expression that constitutes direct incitement or provocation of imminent harmful action may be legitimately punished. Context (audience, immediacy, format) matters in deciding when speech becomes punishable incitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle for conduct: freedom to act so long as no harm to others
rubrics_metrics.description: If he refrains from molesting others in what concerns them, and merely acts according to his own inclination and judgment in things which concern himself, ... he should be allowed, without molestation, to carry his opinions into practice at his own cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions (unlike mere opinion) may be restricted when they unjustifiably harm others. Individuals should have wide latitude to 'experiment' with modes of living so long as they do not make themselves a nuisance or injure others' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to experiment with modes of life (individuality as well‑being)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is desirable ... that free scope should be given to varieties of character, short of injury to others; and that the worth of different modes of life should be proved practically, when any one thinks fit to try them. ... The end of man ... is the highest and most harmonious development of his powers to a complete and consistent whole; that for this there are two requisites, 'freedom, and a variety of situations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should permit diverse, non‑harmful experiments of living because they advance personal development and social progress. Limits are the rights and interests of others; within those limits individuality should be cultivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of self‑determination; harm of blind conformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The human faculties of perception, judgment, discriminative feeling, mental activity, and even moral preference, are exercised only in making a choice. He who does anything because it is the custom, makes no choice. He gains no practice either in discerning or in desiring what is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage individuals to form their own judgments and preferences rather than follow custom unreflectively; doing so exercises and strengthens mental and moral faculties. Excessive conformity produces 'torpid' faculties and weak character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morality of public discussion: candour, fairness, and accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping nothing back which tells, or can be supposed to tell, in their favour. This is the real morality of public discussion ... not exaggerating to their discredit, keeping nothing back which tells, or can be supposed to tell, in their favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate should aim at honest presentation of opponents' views and relevant facts; avoid misrepresentation, suppression, and sophistry. Honour those who fairly present opposing opinions; condemn malignity, bigotry, and deliberate misstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minorities must employ moderation of language to obtain hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions contrary to those commonly received can only obtain a hearing by studied moderation of language, and the most cautious avoidance of unnecessary offence, from which they hardly ever deviate even in a slight degree without losing ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unpopular views generally gain traction through careful, moderate presentation; excessive vituperation alienates potential listeners. Conversely, prevailing opinions often use vituperation to silence minorities, which is unjust and harmful to truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment for instigating tyrannicide: conditions and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The instigation to [tyrannicide], in a specific case, may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed, and at least a probable connection can be established between the act and the instigation. Even then, it is not a foreign government, but the very government assailed, which alone ... can legitimately punish attacks directed against its own existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for violent overthrow may be punishable only where they lead to actual and connected harmful acts; legitimate enforcement is limited to the government affected. This illustrates the general rule limiting punishment to speech with a demonstrable causal link to wrongdoing.
